I wanted to start a discussion regarding https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3422 and what we can do to help move this forward.

This PR has a good starting point for a lot of the problems, but there's a decent amount of issues that are listed in the comments of the PR. It also doesn't entirely make sense for a contributor to come in and start formalizing a problem from scratch seeing that most of the work has already been done. Is there a way we can divide and conquer this PR to make some progress?

I'd like to propose some ideas on actions that we could take and get input from the maintainers and Ryan as well.

1) In the short term, let's focus on just getting the open conjectures checked in since that's the main milestone and it'll help us prioritize.

2) Can we make it so contributors can bite off a chunk of the PR to confirm that the validity of the formalization or make the necessary changes to it and submit that seprately? This is probably more of a question for Ryan. Are you okay with people breaking off chunks of the PR or did you want to commit more time confirming the validity of the mathematical logic?

3) Someone should create a spreadsheet and group up problems that reuse defintions that should be checked into ForMathLib or Mathlib. Then we can be a bit more confident about not redefining the same props and defs.

4) At the end of the day, with 100s of PRs at the ready, the bottleneck is still probably going to be reviews. I'm not entirely sure if we want to blindly let AI review this yet. I'm happy to volunteer to help review, but it also looks like the maintainers have been running AlphaProof just to confirm the validity of some of the formalizations. Are there other methods we could implement to help streamline the review process?

I also would like to see productive use of this pull request

1) I agree, let's focus on the open problems. Although it might make sense to also group them a bit by topic, i.e. when a solved Erdős Problem is very similar to an open one, we might as well add/review both of them at the same time
2) Probably this is a good idea. It should be technically quite easy to keep Ryan as author in the git commit, for instance if one picks out specific problems, one could for instance start with Ryan commits and revert all other files, but the one(s) we are picking.
3) Not sure if a spreadsheet is the right tool here, perhaps better using the github issue systems for that:
It allows to define "Relationship" so one could create an issue with a missing concept that is used in many Erdős Problem, such as "random graph" and then mark the issues we already have as dependent/blocked by this issue.
4) I don't think the review bottleneck is that severe at the moment: yesterday ~all pull requests had received at least one review and typically review takes less than a week. Of course there are some that take way longer, sometimes they are blocking on missing stuff from mathlib or the contributor just become non-responsive for a while, which is ok. It would be absolutely fantastic if you, @Daniel Chin could help more during the review! Also other people are invited to review! Right now I think each reviewer should use their own set of tools, that they are comfortable with. It seems like the same is true for the writing the formalisations, we are seeing handwritten formalisations and many using one form or another of AI help, be it Gemini/Aristotle/Claude Code or whatever.

Currently it seems the best way to obtain a high quality formalisation is to have a good understanding of the underlying math. For some of the conjectures this is easy, because they are elementary. The more non-elementary they get, so more effort it takes to understand the concepts and hence to verify that a faithful formalisation has been obtained.

Another way forward here might be to just split https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3422 into one pull request for each problem (perhaps open problems first), especially if the author is then willing to engage in reviews

1) +1 agree

2) It really depends if Ryan wants to manage / edit in all the feedback from the reviews for each PR, but he should get the feedback anyway, to iterate on the Agent Workflow. I think he should spend more time validating the faithfulness of the statements to ensure / and or improve readeability / reviewability. The model intelligence is much cheaper, than the reviewer time, but of course it's Ryan's Tokens, but its also more about the general outline and the possibility of using a Agentic Workflow to produce very good formalization, which only require small edits / short reviews.

3) +1 on Moritz's Idea

4) I think what Daniel meant, is that for these ~400 open erdos problems, reviewing is certainly the bottleneck, also if this Agentic Workflow performs well, then we can also generalize it to other problems, in which case reviewing will certainly become a more major bottleneck. @Daniel Chin Also AI Reviews would just be for improving the reviewability / readability / correctness, we should not change the standards of the repo, every PR needs a proper review of a maintainer.

Going with the point of Moritz, it might make sense to add a "needs-review" label and let the contributions be mainly concerned with checking mathematical faithfulness. One would have attributions considerations and other issues to address, but it might be a direction we are moving to if creating the code for the formalizations, gets easier and easier.

Hello everyone, thanks for the very spirited discussion and feedback. I just replied on the PR and will do so here as well.

  1. Open problems - grep -R "research open" yields 453 results in the batch I'm working on. Prioritizing those first makes sense to me with respect to the milestone itself.
  2. Attribution - I appreciate the concerns around attribution but I don't believe the added complexity is necessary. There are fancy ways to do this with git but they can get complex fast and my honest view of it is that the AI model did most of "the work" for any given formalization, and therefore I don't feel particularly concerned about another author either just copying / pasting what was there or starting from scratch / prompting a new model. GitHub has the paper trail and if I get a shout-out somewhere for contributing then I'd be a happy camper :)
  3. Organization / Grouping - I've currently got Claude refactoring all conjectures to reuse stuff from the codebase where applicable. Once done, if there are remaining definitions that exist across the new lean conjectures that could be contributed back into the repo, I think passing that task to an agent to identify / consolidate would be doable. No clear need for a spreadsheet approach from my end unless someone would want to take that task on!
  4. Reviews - It does seem to me that human sign-off is still a reasonable standard for each conjecture to land in this repo. There are probably interesting alternatives where a more agent-first directory or repo could accept machine-generated formalizations that pass a certain threshold of machine review, and some org could pay for agents iterating on these things 24/7. I have a physics degree and a very active hobbyist interest in all things math but have been doing mere software development / data engineering work professionally since college and don't currently believe I have a reliable sense of smell for whether a given formalization is "good" or needs work. This is why I'd defer to the more consistent maintainers on what the right approach is for proceeding here.

I'll continue work on an agent pipeline until the results seem good enough to me and to a critical AI reviewer to re-engage on further PRs, suggest further edits to either AGENTS.md, or propose some more comprehensive project around AI formalization of any particular conjecture, Erdos or otherwise.

Thanks for joining the discussion Ryan!

I think in the short term while we wait for your rehash of the PR there's a few things we can do right now.

  • It may be worth it for a human to go through some of your formalizations and pull ones out that look ready to go and get those submitted. That would be a pretty low hanging fruit task for someone who understands the mathematics.
  • It also may be worth it for a human to start looking at the more difficult formalization problems. Specifically, ones that are phrased like "Describe the behavior of f(n)" or "Describe the arithmetic structure" (https://www.erdosproblems.com/1163). These are not phrased as a question easily formalizable in lean so it would be good to see what Claude came up with and see if human would have done the same.
  • Problems that seem tedious or difficult to formalize, I'm more than happy to let your pipeline take first crack at.
  • I know you're iterating on those 453 open problems, but when you feel confident that Claude is giving a reasonable stamp of approval for maybe 10 of them, I say just send out the PR of those 10 so we can start taking a look and give feedback. No need to wait for the completion of all 453.

I'm happy to volunteer for the first task here and just start pulling out formalizations that look good to go with some minor edits.
I'm also going to take a look at 1163 out of curiosity just to see what Claude decided to whip up for it.
Lowest LOC might be an easy criterion for identifying problems that are good candidates for reviews.

Small nitpick, there are 393 open Erdos Problems and 453 formalized statements with category [research open] in Ryans Formalized Statements of Erdos Problems. Might make the mountain of reviews appear a bit smaller :)

Chiming in on the Erdős formalization effort — I have computational ground truth for Problem #114 (Erdős-Herzog-Piranian lemniscate conjecture) that could support a faithful small-n formalization.

What I have: Dual IEEE 1788 rigorous interval arithmetic (Python/mpmath + Rust/inari) verifying that z^(n−1) is the unique maximiser of lemniscate length for 3 ≤ n ≤ 12. All non-extremizer parameter boxes eliminated at level 0 for n ≥ 5; dominance margins 17.1% (n=3) to 71.4% (n=10). Preprint: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19184467

Division of labor as I see it:

  • Small n (3–12): my computational certificate — tractable to formalize via native_decide or a norm_num extension since it reduces to a finite verified computation
  • Large n (> N₀): Tao [2025]'s analytic result — a separate, much harder formalization task I am not attempting
  • Gap (13 ≤ n < N₀): genuinely open, extending my computation further is the obvious next step

Question for the maintainers: Has Ryan's pipeline already produced a Lean statement for #114? If so I'd like to review its mathematical faithfulness. If not, I'm happy to draft the statement for the small-n certificate proof and submit a PR.

PR to teorth/erdosproblems (status update + Zenodo DOI in data): https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/pull/260

cool, @Kenneth Mendoza, to answer your question: yes, @Ryan Tuck's pipeline has produced output for this (as for all other remaining ones): 114 is here:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3422/changes#diff-c0014fd82a4f7e84614d3f3ad1e08e39b6d376b47be56ed8f9dd2e5d1d496699

Thanks @Moritz Firsching — I've reviewed Ryan's 114.lean formalization. A few updates from my end:

Current status: Verification now extends to n = 14 (up from n ≤ 12 at time of my last message). Published certificates for n = 3–13 are at doi:10.5281/zenodo.19322367; the n = 14 result will be in v5. All bounds are IEEE 1788-certified via the inari Rust crate with full certificate chains.

What Ryan's 114.lean currently has:

  • erdos_114 (main conjecture, open)
  • erdos_114_large_n (Tao 2025, solved)
  • erdos_114_deg_two (Eremenko–Hayman 1999, solved)
  • erdos_114_upper_bound (Fryntov–Nazarov 2009, solved)

What's missing: A small-n theorem covering the computationally verified range. I'd like to submit a PR adding erdos_114_small_n for 3 ≤ n ≤ 14 (extending as verification progresses), citing the Zenodo certificate. Since the proof reduces to a finite verified computation, it should be tractable to formalize via native_decide or a norm_num extension.

Happy to coordinate on the statement and review. Would a standalone PR for this be welcome, or should it go through Ryan's batch?
standalone pr would be great!

Hey Moritz @Moritz Firsching I opened the standalone PR for Problem 114 (EHP conjecture) per our last exchange: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3712

It's my first contribution so the CI workflows need maintainer approval to run. CLA is signed.

This is the first of a few I'm planning to submit over the next week or so. Let me know if anything looks off with the file conventions or if you'd want me to adjust the AI disclosure (kept it brief in the Lean docstring, more detail in the Zenodo deposit).

@Moritz Firsching Quick update — I've got a second PR up now: #3745 (Problem 89, distinct distances / Guth-Katz). Learned a few things getting #3712 through — CLA needed my org fork, license URL was http not https, and hausdorffMeasure needed an explicit (1 : ℝ) annotation. This one should be cleaner from the start. Both PRs are ready for CI whenever someone can approve the first-time contributor workflow.

Quick update — two more merged: FC#4036 added Problem 755 (equilateral triangles in ℝ⁶), and FC#4106 was the additive update to 89.lean from your suggestion on #3745: the Erdős–Moser grid upper bound O(n/√log n) next to the existing Guth–Katz variant. Thanks for both reviews.

755 went in tagged research solved — Clemen, Dumitrescu and Liu proved the (1/27 + o(1))n³ bound last year (arXiv:2507.19841), bodies sorry as usual. I couldn't find prior Lean work on counting regular simplices to point a formal_proof attribute at. If anyone knows of any I'd like to add the cite.

On the review bottleneck upthread: I've been building an audit for this. https://williamjblair.github.io/erdos-frontier/ reads each hosted Lean proof (plby, jayyhk) mechanically: its axiom set, plus the Prop hypotheses it takes as parameters, which the case #print axioms cannot see. It also continues the wiki's AI-contributions page that was frozen on June 30. Nine problems so far have claimed proofs that hold only under an unproven result (Maynard-Tao, Kneser, Duke among them); four of those would pass if it was just a plain axiom check. FC#4368, reworked after suggestions from Paul and Moritz, records these hypotheses as structured data on formal_proof.

My #3998 batches come from the same audit. Statements for 199, 224, 226, 246, 296, 363 merged this week (FC#4343); three more batches are in review (FC#4346, FC#4369, FC#4371).

If it would help with review, I can run the audit against any open statement PR. And if a verdict looks wrong, every finding page carries the command to reproduce it. Interested in lots more ideas or suggestions around this too

Ultimately a human (Moritz or Paul or I, most likely ) needs to read each statement carefully. Optimistically count 10min per problem. That's a lower bound of ~200 hours to review all Erdős problems. Anything you can that gets us closer to this theoretical lower bound (by reducing the number of maintainer review cycles required, eg by performing a few review cycles yourself or with an AI) are appreciated
Yes, agreed. Do you have more ideas of what an ideal or better process would look like? ex. how to reduce the cycle time or make review easier?
It has has been great seeing people to start not only contributing, but also reviewing themselves, like @Felix Pernegger, @Daniel Chin and @Jean-Guillaume Durand and others

One thing that has greatly speed up the review is having/imrproving AGETNS.md and README.md files for individual directories (like the ErdosProblems, I'm working on one for Oeis right now..)
After all pretty much what we write during review is repetetive and should just be in a checklist for the Author or their agents to tick off.
For the mathematical correctness tests are key

Right I think perhaps there's ways to better standardize review? Something I've seen on Erdos Problems site is a a maintainer (Nat Sothanaphan) doing a standard check on new reported solutions. Essentially, take the proof and use LLMs in an adversarial fashion to find issues. here is an example

I imagine this would be easy to automate for marginal cost - even if just a single prompt that runs in a cloud container (have seen this with codex or claude code etc)
but agreed on the standard AGENTS.md or checklist etc as foundational

I do want to chime in here and emphasize we probably do need to set up some type of checklist/automated system to help with reviews going forward.

We're definitely seeing a rise in first-time contributors raising PRs that link LLM-formalized proofs for the main Erdos problems and their variants. Historically, most people will post their lean proofs on the Erdos problems website for people to vet and then the website will get updated to reflect that a Lean proof exists.

The PRs are we're seeing recently are Lean proofs that haven't been posted to the Erdos problems website yet or are Lean proofs for the variants of the problems. I'm hoping that the Erdos problems website community can help with a first pass of the Lean formalized proofs in the comments and Tao/Bloom can be in charge of updating the website when a proof is formalized in Lean. The variants are something that we may have to be more responsible for? And with the number of PRs coming in, I definitely think we need some more robust checks and automated reviews.
I have been working in the background on documenting review processes for mathlib with the hope to get AIs to use this info to automatically review PRs at mathlib standards
There are some existing tools for AI reviews of Lean code like (botbaki). Is there some consensus if this is useful yet?

That's great @Yaël Dillies, how do you see it working in the FC repo? On the tooling side, I've been collecting a few suggestions for reducing review cycles in #4394: an author checklist, CI integrity checks on conjectures.json + marking proof conditionality (so a proof that assumes an unproven result isn't read as solved). The last is similar to @Daniel Chin's case, LLM proofs that look complete but aren't.

@Paul Lezeau suggested a review dashboard here like mathlib's queueboard, so I built a prototype demo that shows open PRs by wait time with a fidelity column flagging whether a linked ErdosProblems/N.lean proof is unconditional / conditional / closes-a-gap. This is quite early so want to get more ideas from others about if this would be useful or how to shape it (@Moritz Firsching especially)

If anyone has other ideas for cutting review load, feel free to add them to the issue. Happy to keep collecting them there.

Why not just port the existing reviewer board from mathlib? It is on github etc, so that shouldnt pose a problem.

Good point, I looked into that too (I believe it's this one? queueboard-core). It's a bit more involved than I expected with a Django + Postgres app with a syncer, a reviewer-assignment engine, and a Zulip bot + classification pipeline tuned mostly to mathlib's labels, CI, and scale.

For FC's ~100 open PRs, standing all that up felt like more than we'd need and the mathlib-specific parts wouldn't port cleanly, so I leaned toward something lightweight. That said, I think their review heuristics (PR-state classification, time-in-review) are great and worth borrowing rather than reinventing. Not at all attached to either direction though, and we could start with the queueboard as the base and port from there.
Agree with Felix here, I would advise just to reuse what already exists. Maintaining some custom version will be a pain down the road.

Continuing from this discussion, porting the mathlib queue infrastructure looks easier than I thought.

v2 is already multi-repo: Repository is its own model, queue rules are a per-repo QueueRuleSet. FC would be configuration.

The rendering side is still single-tenant though. Five modules import mathlib_dashboards.py, whose header says it should be a config file. Adding FC means that refactor upstream first, then mapping our labels onto their state classifier, which reads ready-to-merge, delegated and blocked-by-*.

@Moritz Firsching @Paul Lezeau would this be useful? Happy to make an issue and plan for this if so
That's great! I personally think this would be useful (IMO I think we can improve the review process somewhat with such tools). Let's see what @Moritz Firsching thinks!
I think it would be useful -- especially coordinate when more people start reviewing (which is very much the plan: everybody is welcome to review!)
Thanks very generally @Will Blair for all the good work!

Ok here is a starting point: review board for FC and source. I kept simple to maintain and use with just a generate.py and sync.sh file. @Moritz Firsching @Paul Lezeau

It runs queueboard for the fetching (hourly) and state classification, with the default branch and repo URL repointed, and does its own rendering. I kept the frontend simple, but we can easily make any changes there. (as with anything else we want to track/other ideas about how to make it more useful for reviewers)

Where would you like it to live? We could consider

  • transfer the repo to google-deepmind, which keeps the hourly build and its own Pages slot
  • fold it into the FC repo, though there's one Pages deployment per repo and FC's is already the website plus literate source, so it would refresh on the Lean build cadence instead

On the topic of having some LLM reviewer setup, this is something I've been thinking about recently and will start working towards soonish hopefully
I think we could also start building some repo skills here, e.g. perhaps a formalize skill and a review skill to get started.
